p1c5.essay:
Three things happen in this chapter and each undoes the one before: a slip of the tongue, a dream, a coincidence. I think it is the best chapter in Part One and the cruellest, because it gives Raskolnikov a real way out and then takes it back in a paragraph.

The slip first. He is wondering why his feet were carrying him to Razumihin, the one sane and cheerful person he knows, and he hears himself settle the matter: he will go 'on the next day after It, when It will be over'. Then: 'And suddenly he realised what he was thinking.' Garnett's capital I is doing honest work. The thing has no name in his mind, only a pronoun, and the pronoun has already been entered in his diary like an appointment. Dostoevsky's psychology runs this way throughout. Decisions get made somewhere below the place where Raskolnikov argues, and he finds out about them afterwards, like a man opening his own post.

Then the dream, which I find close to unbearable, and which is written with a patience the rest of the book rarely allows itself. Look at how long Dostoevsky spends on the approach: the flat town 'bare as the hand', the black dust of the road, the church with the green cupola, the rice pudding with raisins laid out in a cross, the baby brother's grave the boy kisses. All of it is in place before a single blow falls, so that the violence arrives in a world where a seven-year-old still has a father's hand to hold and a habit of reverence. Then Mikolka, 'red as a carrot', and a cart built for a dray horse with a thin sorrel mare in the shafts. The horror is partly the beating and partly the mood of the thing. It is a holiday. People laugh; a fat woman cracks nuts from start to finish; somebody calls for a song. Mikolka's defence, shouted three times, is 'my property', and nobody has an answer to it, including the old man who asks whether he is a Christian and then cannot help smiling when the mare tries to kick.

The usual question is who Raskolnikov is in this dream, and the usual answer is everyone: the child with his arms round the dead head, Mikolka with the crowbar, and (some readers add) the mare herself, harnessed to more than she can pull. I mostly agree, but the figure who stays with me is the father. 'They are drunk.... They are brutal... it's not our business!' That is the voice of decent, ordinary helplessness, and the boy cannot breathe inside it. A month of theorising in the garret has been, among other things, a refusal of that sentence. He wants it to be his business: his sister's engagement in [[p1c3|his mother's letter]], the girl on the boulevard in [[p1c4]], the Marmeladovs in [[p1c2]]. The dream shows him where the wish to rescue and the wish to strike both come from, and how tangled together they are.

He wakes and says it plainly for the first time, axe and skull and 'sticky warm blood', and his whole body refuses. This matters. The reasoning is still, he says, 'true as arithmetic'; nothing in the argument has been refuted. He simply cannot do it. And for the length of one sunset on the bridge he is well: the abscess has burst, he prays, he looks calmly at the Neva. If this were only a novel of ideas it would have to go on arguing. Dostoevsky lets the body and the childhood win outright, and then shows how little the victory is worth.

For now the narrator steps back, into 'later on, when he recalled that time', and tells us Raskolnikov took an unnecessary turn through the Hay Market. There he overhears a huckster inviting the pawnbroker's sister to tea: tomorrow, seven o'clock. That is all. An accident of the pavement, and the man who had just renounced his 'accursed... dream' goes home 'like a man condemned to death', feeling he has 'no more freedom of thought, no will'. I do not quite believe him, and I don't think Dostoevsky does either. Nothing has been decided for him. A piece of information has made the thing convenient, and he experiences convenience as fate. The narrator's word is 'superstitiously'. Hold on to it, because [[p1c6|the next chapter]] begins by taking the Hay Market conversation apart and showing how ordinary it was.

annotations.quote: I shall go to him... on the next day after It, when It will be over and everything will begin afresh
annotations.note: He has not decided anything, as far as he knows, and yet here is a calendar with the deed already on it. The capital I is the translator's way of marking a thing he cannot name. Notice also the fantasy tucked in at the end: afterwards 'everything will begin afresh', as if It were a door into a new life.

annotations.quote: The flowers especially caught his attention; he gazed at them longer than at anything.
annotations.note: A small sentence I would not skip. Out on the islands, away from the stench and the taverns, the first thing this would-be man of iron does is stare at flowers through a fence. Dostoevsky keeps showing us the person the theory has to get past.

annotations.quote: the dreamer, were he an artist like Pushkin or Turgenev even, could never have invented them in the waking state
annotations.note: A sly bit of stage management. Dostoevsky is about to write the dream himself, so he clears his throat by saying no artist could invent one this convincing, and names a living rival while he is at it. Then he goes and does it.

annotations.quote: The woman went on cracking nuts and laughing.
annotations.note: For me the most frightening figure in the dream, more than Mikolka. He at least is in a rage. She is simply having a nice holiday, and the sound of nutshells runs under the whole beating.

annotations.quote: It’s my property, I’ll do what I choose.
annotations.note: Mikolka's entire moral philosophy, and he says it three times. Listen for how it rhymes with the questions the book has been raising since the first chapter: who has the right to dispose of another creature's life, and on what grounds.

annotations.quote: put his arms round her bleeding dead head and kissed it, kissed the eyes and kissed the lips
annotations.note: Earlier in the dream the same child kisses his baby brother's grave 'religiously and reverently'. The gesture is repeated here on the mare. Whatever else Raskolnikov has become, this boy is still somewhere in him, and the dream has just proved it to him.

annotations.quote: that all that I have concluded this last month is clear as day, true as arithmetic
annotations.note: Read this carefully: he does not say he was wrong. The logic stands and he recoils anyway, which leaves the logic sitting there intact. 'Arithmetic' is a word to listen for in [[p1c6]].

annotations.quote: It was as though an abscess that had been forming for a month past in his heart had suddenly broken.
annotations.note: The plan as an infection, the renunciation as lancing it. The medical language is everywhere in this book (fever, shivering, 'morbid'), and it raises a question Dostoevsky never quite settles: is the idea making him ill, or is illness producing the idea?

annotations.quote: As though it had been lying in wait for him on purpose!
annotations.note: The voice here is the narrator's but the feeling is Raskolnikov's, looking back from some later time. He needs the Hay Market meeting to have been an ambush by fate. The alternative is that he walked into it.

annotations.quote: he felt suddenly in his whole being that he had no more freedom of thought, no will
annotations.note: An hour ago, on the bridge, the cry was 'Freedom, freedom!' Now he feels he has none. Both feelings are sincere. What interests me is that the loss of freedom arrives as a kind of relief from having to choose.

links.why: His mother's letter asks whether he still prays as he did as a child; the dream goes back to that child and to the father she mentions.
The walk that ends in the bushes on Petrovsky Ostrov begins here, with the girl on the boulevard and the twenty copecks he is still counting.
The 'experiment' he remembers on waking is the visit to the pawnbroker in the opening chapter, down to the nausea on the stairs.
The next chapter opens by explaining what the Hay Market invitation was actually about, and where the idea first came from.

p1c6.essay:
This chapter runs backwards before it runs forwards, and the order matters. Having ended [[p1c5]] on what felt like fate, Dostoevsky opens by letting the air out of it: Lizaveta was being asked to price some second-hand clothes, 'a very ordinary matter'. Then he goes back six weeks to a tavern where Raskolnikov, fresh from his first sight of the pawnbroker, hears a student at the next table make the whole case. One useless, spiteful old woman against a hundred lives; 'simple arithmetic'; the life of a louse. It is disconcerting to learn that the great idea is common property, the kind of thing students say between games of billiards. Raskolnikov takes the coincidence as a 'guiding hint'. I take it as Dostoevsky telling us that the idea was in the Petersburg air, and that what sets his hero apart is only that he went on thinking it. The officer, who is no philosopher, punctures the speech with one question: would you do it yourself? 'Of course not!' And they go back to their game.

The second half is all objects and clock time, and it is where the book turns into a thriller. The noose sewn under the left armhole, designed 'a fortnight before'. The fake pledge, wood and iron wrapped 'carefully and daintily' in white paper, with a knot meant to be slow. I find these details more damning than any of the theory, because they are so pleased with themselves. And yet the same pages insist that he never believed in any of it, that his resolutions looked more absurd the more final they became. Both are true together. He has prepared the props and not the act, and he has a theory to cover the gap: criminals fail because will and reason desert them like an illness, but his will not, since what he plans is 'not a crime'. The narrator declines to walk us through how he reached that, a little too smoothly ('we have run too far ahead already'). Keep the omission in mind.

Then the plan meets the world and fails at once. Nastasya is in the kitchen hanging out linen, so there is no axe. What rescues him is a glint under the porter's bench, and his comment is the best line in the chapter: 'When reason fails, the devil helps!' From there he walks across town thinking about fountains, and the chapter stops with his hand on the bell and someone else's ear against the other side of the door.

annotations.quote: A strange idea was pecking at his brain like a chicken in the egg, and very, very much absorbed him.
annotations.note: Note the order of events. The idea is already pecking before the student at the next table opens his mouth. What Raskolnikov will call a mysterious coincidence is a man hearing his own half-formed thought said aloud by a stranger.

annotations.quote: She is such a soft, gentle creature, ready to put up with anything, always willing, willing to do anything.
annotations.note: The argument that follows is about the old woman, but look how much of the tavern talk is about Lizaveta, and in what tone: relish, laughter, a request to have her do some mending. Everybody uses her. The student is no exception.

annotations.quote: One death, and a hundred lives in exchange--it’s simple arithmetic!
annotations.note: Here is the argument in its plainest form, and the word Raskolnikov used on waking from the dream in [[p1c5]]. It is worth asking who is doing the sum and who appointed him. The speech never raises that.

annotations.quote: if you would not do it yourself, there’s no justice about it
annotations.note: The officer's whole contribution, and I think the shrewdest sentence in the chapter. A principle you would not act on is talk. It cuts in an uncomfortable direction, though: it implies that the man who would do it has something the talker lacks.

annotations.quote: blue, cold water running among the parti-coloured stones and over the clean sand which glistened here and there like gold
annotations.note: In a novel of dust, heat and stairwells, this is the one clean cold thing, and it exists only in a daydream on the afternoon in question. 'Parti-coloured' is Garnett's period word for many-coloured. He is drinking apart from the caravan, alone even here.

annotations.quote: the more final they were, the more hideous and the more absurd they at once became in his eyes
annotations.note: An odd and very true observation about how he has kept the plan alive: by never finishing it. Each loose end lets him go on treating it as a thought. The narrator adds that had everything been settled he would have dropped it as monstrous.

annotations.quote: for the simple reason that his design was “not a crime....”
annotations.note: The quotation marks are his, the four dots are the narrator trailing off. We are told the conclusion and refused the reasoning. Dostoevsky is holding something back on purpose, and it is the most important thing we do not yet know about this young man.

annotations.quote: “When reason fails, the devil helps!” he thought with a strange grin.
annotations.note: A proverb, tossed off, and the grin is 'strange' because he half means it. Count the lucky accidents from here to the end of the chapter and ask whom they are lucky for.

annotations.quote: So probably men led to execution clutch mentally at every object that meets them on the way
annotations.note: Dostoevsky knew. In 1849 he was taken to a Petersburg parade ground with other political prisoners to be shot, and reprieved at the last minute. The detail of a mind fastening on fountains and gardens is reported from the inside. Notice too which of the two people in this story Raskolnikov compares himself to.

annotations.quote: just as he was doing on the outside was secretly listening within
annotations.note: Two people a door's thickness apart, each with an ear to the wood, each pretending not to be there. It is a wonderfully held image, and Dostoevsky likes it enough to use it again in [[p1c7|the next chapter]].

links.why: The 'experiment' and the promised silver cigarette case both come from that first visit, as does the worry about his conspicuous hat.
The overheard invitation in the Hay Market, which this chapter opens by explaining, and his own use of 'arithmetic' the afternoon before.
The reasoning the narrator skips here, about crime and who is entitled to commit it, is finally argued out loud in this chapter.

p1c7.essay:
The thing the book has circled for six chapters takes about a page, and the first surprise is how little of the chapter it fills. Everything Raskolnikov prepared works: the knot holds the old woman at the window and her back turns. And the blow, when it comes, is described as if nobody struck it: 'almost without effort, almost mechanically', and then, 'He seemed not to use his own strength in this.' After a month of asking whether he could will this act, the act happens almost in the passive voice. I don't read that as Dostoevsky making excuses for him. It is an exact report of how a man does what he cannot believe he is doing, and it leaves open the question the rest of the book will worry at, which is what in him did this.

Then look at what we are made to see. The hair 'thickly smeared with grease', the rat's-tail plait, the broken horn comb. Dostoevsky will not let her be the louse of the tavern argument in [[p1c6]], and he will not make her lovable either; she is a particular old woman with a particular comb. The same goes for the crosses on the purse string and the bedroom with its 'whole shrine of holy images'. The student's arithmetic had her money going uselessly to a monastery. Here is what that item in the sum looked like from inside her flat.

And then the plan, such as it was, runs out. For me this is the chapter's real subject: the distance between a theory and ten minutes in a room. He tries keys he can see will not fit. He wipes his hands on red brocade because 'on red blood will be less noticeable', and catches himself thinking it. He fills his pockets with a few parcels without looking at them and leaves the chest of drawers unopened. The man who wondered in the last chapter why criminals lose their heads, and exempted himself, has become a specimen for his own theory before the body is cold.

Lizaveta is the centre of it. She was supposed to be at the Hay Market drinking tea; the whole sensation of fate at the end of [[p1c5]] rested on her absence. She walks in through a door he never shut. I find her death the hardest passage in the novel to read, harder than the dream of the mare, which it deliberately recalls: a creature that does not defend itself, a blow to the head. Dostoevsky gives her mouth the twitch of a frightened baby's and has her hold out 'her empty left hand', not even towards her face. Notice too that the old woman got the blunt side of the axe and Lizaveta gets the edge. No theory covers this. Nobody at the billiard table argued that the gentle sister, the one everybody exploited, should die so that a hundred lives might be saved. The narrator's phrase is 'this second, quite unexpected murder', and the flatness of 'unexpected' is devastating. A few lines on we are told that if he had been able to think, he might have gone and given himself up, 'not from fear, but from simple horror and loathing of what he had done'. Keep that sentence. It says the loathing was there from the first minute.

The second half is pure suspense, and Dostoevsky is better at it than people who think of him only as a novelist of ideas tend to allow. The open door. The steps coming up from the bottom of the stairs, 'heavy, even and unhurried'. Then the mirror image of the last chapter's ending: two men with a door between them, only now Raskolnikov is the one inside, watching a hook jump in its catch. I admit that I want him to get away, every time I read it. I think the chapter is built to produce that wish and then leave the reader to live with having had it. The young man outside, who works out from the clank of the hook that somebody must be within, is 'studying the law'. So, until recently, was Raskolnikov.

He escapes by a string of flukes: Koch's impatience, the painters tearing downstairs after one another, an empty flat with wet paint on the floor. He even puts the axe back. None of it is skill. He ends where [[p1c1|the book found him]], in the garret, on the sofa, with 'scraps and shreds of thoughts' he cannot hold.

annotations.quote: again two sharp and suspicious eyes stared at him out of the darkness
annotations.note: 'As before', 'again': the scene is staged as a repeat of the rehearsal visit in [[p1c1]], same crack of the door, same eyes. The difference is that this time he grabs the door and nearly pulls her out onto the landing. The plan starts going wrong in its first second.

annotations.quote: He seemed not to use his own strength in this.
annotations.note: The most important sentence about the act itself. All through Part One things have been said and decided 'of themselves' in him; here the pattern reaches its end point. And the next clause is chilling: once the axe has come down, 'his strength returned to him'.

annotations.quote: fastened by a broken horn comb which stood out on the nape of her neck
annotations.note: The camera is exactly where his eyes are, on the back of her head, and it records a cheap broken comb. A weaker novelist would have looked away or looked at him. Dostoevsky makes the victim most real in the instant she is struck.

annotations.quote: On the string were two crosses, one of Cyprus wood and one of copper, and an image in silver filigree
annotations.note: Garnett's 'Cyprus wood' is cypress. He takes the purse and flings the crosses back on the body, an action that says more than he knows. I would remember that these objects were here and what he did with them.

annotations.quote: “It’s red, and on red blood will be less noticeable,” the thought passed through his mind
annotations.note: A flash of idiot cunning, and he hears it as such at once. It is the first clear sign that the cool reasoner he expected to be in this room is not the one who turned up.

annotations.quote: She only put up her empty left hand, but not to her face, slowly holding it out before her as though motioning him away.
annotations.note: The gesture I cannot get past. The narrator has just pointed out that covering her face was 'the most necessary and natural action', and a lifetime of being beaten has taken even that from her. She meets an axe the way she met everything.

annotations.quote: not from fear, but from simple horror and loathing of what he had done
annotations.note: The narrator steps outside Raskolnikov for a moment to tell us what he would have done had he been able to think. It is easy to read past in the rush. The distinction between fear and loathing is one the book means to hold him to.

annotations.quote: They were now standing opposite one another, as he had just before been standing with the old woman
annotations.note: Dostoevsky points out his own symmetry. An hour ago he was the visitor listening at the door and she was the one inside. He has taken her place in the flat, and the narration wants us to feel it.

annotations.quote: I’m studying the law you see! It’s evident, e-vi-dent there’s something wrong here!
annotations.note: Almost comic, this bright young man relishing his deduction about the hook. But he is right, and he is a student of the same subject Raskolnikov gave up. It is the first time anyone reasons about the crime from the outside, and it takes him half a minute.

annotations.quote: If the porter had asked him, “What do you want?” he would perhaps have simply handed him the axe.
annotations.note: After all that planning, his safety at the end hangs on a porter being out twice in one evening. The picture of him simply handing the axe over is funny and terrible, and it tells you how thin the line is between concealing and blurting.

links.why: The rehearsal: the same door opened a crack, the same keys in the right-hand pocket, and what he said to himself on the stairs afterwards.
Set Lizaveta's death beside the dream of the mare, and recall that it was her Hay Market appointment that seemed to settle everything.
His theory that criminals fail through a collapse of will and reason, from which he excused himself, and the student's 'simple arithmetic'.
Part Two picks up on the same sofa, with the scraps and shreds of thought he cannot catch hold of here.
